node.label: Alice Kessler-Harris
node.date_label: Out to Work (1982) · A Woman’s Wage (1990) · In Pursuit of Equity (2001) · Gendering Labor History (2007)
node.description: In In Pursuit of Equity (2001), Alice Kessler-Harris argues that gendered assumptions about breadwinning and family dependence shaped apparently fair employment and welfare policies, limiting women’s economic citizenship. Out to Work (1982) traces the transformation of women’s work into paid labour, examining how class, race, ethnicity and assumptions about wage-earning and family roles shaped that process. A Woman’s Wage (1990; updated edition 2014) examines how disputes over minimum wages, equal pay and comparable worth produce and challenge gendered social values. Gendering Labor History (2007) brings together her interventions on unions, gender, class and social policy. Reviewing that collection in 2009, Francisca de Haan praises its account of gender and class while calling its proposal to share or socialize household care perhaps utopian. The criticism qualifies that proposal rather than rejecting the collection’s historical analysis.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Women Have Always Worked (1981; revised second edition, A Concise History, 2018); Out to Work (1982; anniversary edition listed by OUP in 2003); A Woman’s Wage (1990; second edition with added epilogue, 2014); U.S. History as Women’s History (1995), coedited with Linda K. Kerber and Kathryn Kish Sklar; In Pursuit of Equity (2001); Gendering Labor History (2007); A Difficult Woman (2012).

proposed_edges.relationship: In the 2019 interview, Kessler-Harris credits Gerda Lerner as a major influence in her turn toward women’s history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: LaborOnline excerpts, paragraph beginning “I discovered the newly organized”; “a major influence in my life.” Retrospective self-report; full Jewish Social Studies interview unread. Lerner is another candidate in entries.json.
proposed_edges.map_label: Lerner and the turn to women’s history

proposed_edges.relationship: Kessler-Harris and Linda K. Kerber coedited U.S. History as Women’s History (1995), with Kathryn Kish Sklar.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01). CV p. 3. The UNC Press page returned 403 to me. Extra support: the In Pursuit of Equity acknowledgments, p. xi (licensed preview), say 'Linda Kerber and Kathryn Kish Sklar, my coeditors of U.S. History as Women's History, helped to clarify the argument that appeared in that volume and became a part of chapter 3', and p. x thanks Kerber for 'intellectual companionship and willingness to offer acute criticism'. Apply the co-editing convention (contribution, undirected). Optionally add akh_equity_2001 to source_ids. Phrase seen: “U.S. History as Women's History, University of North Carolina Press, l995. edited with Linda K. Kerber and Kathryn Kish Sklar” Read at: https://professorsemeritus.columbia.edu/sites/default/files/content/CVs%20for%20Fellows%20Directory/Alice%20Kessler-Harris.pdf

proposed_edges.relationship: In In Pursuit of Equity (2001), Kessler-Harris relies on Cott's account of 1920s feminists' disputes over whether economic equality was an appropriate goal to set up her argument about economic citizenship.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Licensed publisher preview (In Pursuit of Equity, 2001), introduction p. 4 and n. 12: 'And into the 1920s, historian Nancy Cott tells us, different kinds of feminists disputed bitterly over whether economic equality was an appropriate goal.' Cott is also thanked as a reader of the manuscript (acknowledgments, p. xi). Read by Fable (F02-009); book body otherwise unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Eileen Boris reports, Kessler-Harris’s 1993 review of Skocpol’s Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992) questions the paternalism/maternalism divide because both camps supported a male breadwinner family wage.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Boris’s 4 August 1994 posting, first two substantive sentences: “the same family wage.” Chappell’s displayed notes 38/42 date the review to December 1993; Boris’s “earlier this year” is imprecise. Original review unread; mediated attribution only. Skocpol is another candidate.

proposed_edges.relationship: Kessler-Harris and Carroll Smith-Rosenberg coedited Women in Culture and Politics: A Century of Change (1986), with Judith Friedlander and Blanche Wiesen Cook.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author CV, printed p. 3, edited-books entry names all four. Bibliographic collaboration only; collection body unread. Smith-Rosenberg is another candidate in entries.json.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Francisca de Haan reports, Kessler-Harris invokes E. H. Carr in the introduction to Gendering Labor History (2007) to defend history prompted by present questions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: De Haan (2009), paragraph beginning “The essays are preceded,” citing collection p. 3: “challenging events of the day.” Named-reader attribution; original introduction and Carr passage unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Gendering Labor History (2007), Kessler-Harris reframes women’s limited union membership as a question about exclusion by employers and male unions, as de Haan explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: De Haan, pp. 111–113, opening-essay discussion, citing collection pp. 23–25: “kept out.” Review read; original 1975 essay and 2007 reprint unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gendering Labor History (2007) makes masculinity and the interaction of gender and class part of explaining labour and social policy, as de Haan argues.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: De Haan, paragraphs on Parts 2–3: “mutual interaction.” Named-reader evidence; individual essays unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Gender and class shape labour history

proposed_edges.relationship: Kessler-Harris coedited U.S. History as Women’s History (1995) and contributed its chapter on the construction of the 1939 Social Security amendments, “Designing Women and Old Fools.”
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UNC publisher description and contributor list name her topic. CV p. 4 identifies her chapter, “Designing Women and Old Fools.” Chapter body unread; no further chapter argument asserted.
proposed_edges.map_label: Women in Social Security policy (1995 chapter)

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Feminism and the Making of Canadian Working-Class History” (2000), Joan Sangster cites Alice Kessler-Harris’s call in “A New Agenda for American Labor History” (1989) to treat gender, like class, as a historical process as symptomatic of feminist labour history’s move away from subordinating gender to class.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 140–142 and note 48 in the journal PDF. The body explicitly engages the framework; the note identifies the 1989 and 1993 essays. This is specific historiographical use. Those essays were not independently read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Gender as a historical process in Sangster’s historiography

proposed_edges.relationship: Gendering Labor History (2007) contributes to global history through its concluding essay on women’s wage labour, which Francisca de Haan’s 2009 review identifies as an attempt to examine gender within a global history of women’s paid work.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on the journal publisher’s page. De Haan explicitly assesses the concluding essay’s global scope. The claim concerns the 2007 collection as reviewed; neither the collection nor the earlier version of that essay was independently read. This is a bounded contribution, not a founding claim.
proposed_edges.map_label: Gender in global histories of women’s paid work
